title: The fierce one who heals
hookLine: a Vedic poet bows to the fierce, braided-haired god, and asks him to heal
carry: rudra the fierce is shiva, the kind
tomorrow: what did a poor boy want more than milk?

cards: A prayer for a village can be very practical. Keep the children well. Keep the animals healthy.
Let nobody fall sick. In the Rig Veda, a poet brings exactly that kind of prayer to Rudra, the fierce god whose names Shiva carries.
And before he asks for anything, he names him: strong, and kapardin, the one with braided, coiled hair. This is a god people were afraid of. So why go to him for medicine?

teach.b: Kaparda is a braid or coil of hair, and kapardin is the one who wears it, the same piled locks you still see on Shiva today.

In the Rig Veda, Rudra is the fierce one, a god of the wild places, with arrows people pray will miss them. In this very hymn the poet begs him: don't harm our children, our cattle, our people; don't strike in anger.

teach.h: HIS ARROWS FEARED, HIS MEDICINES IN HAND.
teach.b: And yet the same hymn pictures him holding healing medicines in his hand, and another hymn calls him the greatest healer of all healers. The village doesn't run from the frightening god.
It bows to him, by name, and asks for the gentle side of the same power. Out of that grows one of the oldest teachings about Shiva.

The word shiva first meant kind, auspicious, gracious, and the Vedic poets prayed for Rudra's shiva form, his kind form. Over time, scholars and teachers note, the hope became the name. The fierce one is the kind one.
Hindu worship doesn't split God into a good god and a scary one.

teach.h: THE RUDRAM BOWS TO HIS ANGER.
teach.b: The Shri Rudram, a Vedic litany of Rudra's names still chanted when water is poured over the Shiva linga, opens by bowing to his anger and his arrow, and asks that they turn kind.

teach.h: THE FIERCE ONE IS THE KIND ONE.
teach.b: Many teachers read it as a way to pray with your fear, not around it: name the frightening thing, bow, and ask for grace. Families still have the Rudram chanted for health and for blessings on a home.
A village asking to be well, all over again.

how: Images of Shiva keep his coiled, matted hair, and the Shri Rudram, the Vedic litany that opens by bowing to Rudra's anger, is chanted as water and milk are poured over the Shiva linga.

o: a hymn of Shiva's names, here the fierce god who heals
a hymn asking Rudra to leave the village forever
a Vedic rule that priests must never cut their hair

games.q: you're a Vedic poet. your village needs to stay healthy, and the god you need is Rudra: fierce, wild, with arrows everyone fears. what do you do?
o: avoid him and pray to a gentler god.
bow to him by name and ask for his healing side.
ask him to aim his arrows at a rival village.
games.why: the poet names him strong and braided-haired, begs him to spare the children and cattle, and pictures healing medicines in his hand.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you're afraid of right now, a test, a worry about someone's health. Don't push it away. On the in-breath, name it plainly.
On the out-breath, bow to it inwardly and hand it over, asking for healing and steadiness for everyone it touches.
If you pray, you can pour a little water, the way families do over the Shiva linga, and say Om Namah Shivaya; if you don't, simply wish the people in your home well.

wordCard.voice: The Shiva Sahasranama. Today's name from it: Kapardin, the one with coiled, braided hair, the fierce Vedic god a village asked for healing.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Kapardin, the one who wears kaparda, coiled or braided hair; a Vedic word for Rudra and a name of Shiva.

carryVoice: Your line: Rudra the fierce is Shiva, the kind. Hindus bow to the fierce face of God and ask for the gentle one. See you tomorrow.
